---
title: "Keep Calm and Quarantine On?"
subtitle: "How vaccination and infection control shape border quarantine effectiveness"
author: "Aatish Prasad"
date: "2026-10-12"
categories: [news]
---

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia relied on border quarantine to reduce the risk of infected travellers bringing the virus into the wider community. However, keeping the virus contained became more challenging as new variants, such as Delta, spread more easily. Vaccines offered another layer of protection, but their ability to prevent infection varied, and vaccination alone could not guarantee that the virus would remain contained.

This raised an important question: could vaccination make border quarantine sufficiently safe, or were strong infection-control measures still essential? Zachreson et al. (2022) investigated this issue by using computer simulations to examine how the virus's ability to spread, vaccine effectiveness, vaccination levels in the wider community and quarantine controls influenced the risk of an infection escaping into the community and triggering an outbreak.

![](thumbnail.jpg)



Published in Science Advances in 2022, the study used computer simulations to model a hypothetical quarantine hotel with 100 travellers and 20 vaccinated staff (Zachreson et al., 2022). The researchers tested how viral transmissibility, vaccine effectiveness and infection-control measures affected the risk of infections escaping quarantine and triggering community outbreaks.

The model was compared with Australian data, which recorded 14 quarantine breaches in a year, nine of which led to further spread. The simulation produced roughly twice as many breaches, suggesting it was more useful for comparing scenarios than predicting exact numbers (Zachreson et al., 2022).

The simulation showed that quarantine safety depends on four things working together.

**A more contagious virus needs a stronger vaccine.** Compared with the early pandemic (no vaccines, a virus passing to about 3 people on average), a Delta-like virus (about 6 people) needed a vaccine that was over 60% effective just to keep the risk of infection escaping quarantine at the old level. At about 8 people it needed over 70%. For even more contagious viruses the requirement levelled off at 70–80% .

**Vaccinating the community buys time.** If the vaccine was weak (under about 60% effective), vaccinating more people made little difference. If it was 80% effective or better and community coverage was high, the time until an outbreak had a 50% chance of starting grew from about 15 days to around 1,000 days, nearly three years . That’s a long delay, but the risk was pushed back, not removed.\

**Strict hotel hygiene still mattered.** When protections inside the hotel were weakened, the chance of an infected person leaving quarantine jumped, up to 100 times higher with a very contagious virus and a weak vaccine.

Together, these results show that vaccination made quarantine safer but couldn’t do the job alone.
